etymology: First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1762. Short form of names like {{m|sv|Adela}}, and of biblical {{der|sv|he|-}} origin.
From {{der|sv|he|אָדָם||tr=adam|earth, man, soil, light brown}}.
From {{w|Runic Swedish}} {{m|gmq-osw|Aulfr}}.
From {{der|sv|la|Hadrianus}}, ultimately from {{der|sv|ett|𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀}}.
{{der|sv|non|Agni}}, short form of compound names beginning with ''Agn''-, from {{m|non|age||awe}} or {{m|non|egg||point of a weapon}}. Cognate to German [[Egon]].
{{bor+|sv|la|Agneta}}, diminutive form of {{m|la|Agnes}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1397. Cognate with {{cog|da|Agnete}}.
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|fi|Aina}}, first recorded as a name of Swedish speaking Finns in 1839, in Sweden in 1845.
First recorded in Sweden in 1283. Cognate with German and English {{l|en|Albert}}.
A feminine form of {{m|sv|Albert}} popularized by 17th- and 18th-century royalty. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1691.
From {{der|sv|la|Albīnus}}, partly merged with {{der|sv|gem}} [[Albwin]], the German equivalent of English {{m|en|Alvin}}.
Equivalent to English {{l|en|Alexander}}. First recorded in Sweden ([[Scania]]) in 1201.
From {{bor|sv|grc|Ἀλεξάνδρα}}. Feminine form of {{m|sv|Alexander}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Alfr}}. Also a contraction of {{m|sv|Adolf}}.
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|en|Alfred}}, from {{der|sv|ang|Ælfræd}}. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1751.
From {{der|sv|non|Algautr}}, from {{m|non|alfr||elf}} + {{m|non|gautr||Geat}}.
From {{bor|sv|en|Alice}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1841.
Latinate variant of {{m|sv|Alice}}.
From {{bor|sv|en|Allan}} in the 19th century.
From {{der|sv|non|Alfrekr||elf-ruler}}, the name of a mythical king. The name has also absorbed {{der|sv|goh|Adalric||noble ruler}}, and {{l|sv|Alarik||all-ruler}}, the name of the Visigoth king.
A 19th century feminine form of [[Alf]], or a short form of female compound names beginning with Alf-, such as [[Alfhild]] and [[Alfrida]].
{{der+|sv|la|Amanda}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1735.
Vernacular form of {{m|sv|Andreas}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1396.
From {{der|sv|la|Andreas}}, of {{der|sv|grc|-}} origin. First recorded in Sweden in [[rune]]s in the 12th century.
{{nonlemma}}
From {{der|sv|la|angelica}}.
From {{der|sv|es|Anita}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1864.
From {{der|sv|en|Ann}}, first recorded as a Swedish given name in 1860.
Phonetic rendering of the {{der|sv|fr|-}} pronunciation of {{m|sv|Anne-Christine}}.

First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1291. {{inh+|sv|gmq-osw|Anna}}, from {{der|sv|la-vul|Anna}}, from {{der|sv|grc|Ἄννα|}}, equal to the {{der|sv|he|-}} female name {{m|he|חַנָּה|tr=ḥannâ}} of Old Testament, meaning "grace, gracious". Cognate with English [[Ann]].
{{com+|sv|Anna|Karin}}.
From {{bor|sv|fr|Anne}}. First recorded as a given name of Swedes in 1773.

From [[Anders]], [[Anton]], [[Arne]]. {{glossary|Affix}} of the two first letters {{af|sv|An-|n|-e|t2=[[gemination]]|t3=[[hypocoristic]] [[suffix]]}}.

From {{bor|sv|fr|Annette}}.
From {{der|sv|en|Annie}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1843.
A {{gl|diminutive}} of {{m|sv|Anna}}. First attested in Sweden in 1521.
From {{der|sv|la|Antonius}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1623. Cognate with {{cog|en|Anthony}}.

From {{inh|sv|non|Ǫnundr}}, Runic Swedish {{m|non|ᛅᚾᚢᚾᛏᚱ}}, {{m|non|ᚬᚾᚢᚾᛏᚱ}}.<ref>[https://kulturbilder.wordpress.com/2013/10/27/runstenar-uppland-u-661/amp/ Runestone U 661]</ref><ref>[https://kulturbilder.wordpress.com/2015/08/05/runstenar-vastergotland-vg-6/amp/ Runestone Vg 6]</ref> Cognate with {{cog|no|Ånund}} and {{cog|is|Önundur}}.
{{der|sv|non|Arni}}. A [[runic]] name revived in 1862.
{{inh|sv|gmq-osw|[[Arnvidh]], [[Arvidh]]}}, from {{inh|sv|non|Arnviðr}}.
{{inh|sv|non|Ásgeirr}}, from {{m|non|áss||god}} + {{m|non|geirr||spear}}. Cognate with {{cog|fo,is|Ásgeir}}, {{cog|nn|Åsgeir}}, {{cog|da|Asger}}, {{cog|de|Ansgar}}, and {{cog|en|Oscar}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Askr}}, from {{m|non|askr||ash tree}}.
From {{m|sv|ask||ash tree}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Ǫzurr||answerer}}.
{{inh+|sv|gmq-osw|Astrīþ}}, from {{w|Runic Swedish}} {{m|gmq-osw|Asfriþ}}, from {{der|sv|non|Ástríðr}}. Occurs in Norse mythology, revived in Sweden in 1820.
From {{der|sv|la|Augustus}}.

{{ety|sv|:der|la:Augusta}}
From {{der|sv|la|Augusta}}, feminine of {{m|la|Augustus}}.
From {{der|sv|da|Aksel}}, {{m|da|Axel}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1371.
Medieval vernacular form of the saint's name {{m|sv|Barbara}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1484.
From {{bor|sv|la|Beāta}}.
Contraction of {{der|sv|la-lat|Benedictus}}. First recorded in Sweden as ''Benkt'' in 1364. Cognate with {{cog|da|Bent}} and {{cog|en|Bennett}}.
Medieval equivalent of modern German {{m|de|Berthold}}, from {{der|sv|gem}} ''[[berht]]'' "bright" + ''[[wald]]'' "rule". First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1396.
From {{der|sv|en|Bill}}. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1895.
From {{bor|sv|en|Billy}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Birgir||helper}}.
Short form of {{m|sv|Birgitta}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1879.
From {{der|sv|sga|Brigit}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1293. Cognate with {{cog|en|Bridget}}.
{{clipping|sv|Birgitte}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Bjarni}}, short form of names starting with {{m|non||Bjarn-}}, from {{m|non|bjǫrn||bear}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Bjǫrn}}, from {{m|non|bjǫrn||bear}}, with identical meaning in modern Swedish. Runic name revived since 1816. Cognate with Danish and Norwegian {{m|da|Bjørn}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Búi||dweller, long-time resident}}, originally a medieval byname.

{{glossary|Affix}} of {{af|sv|Bo|-s|s|-e|t2=[[genitive]]|t3=[[gemination]]|t4=[[hypocoristic]] [[suffix]]}}.

Short form of {{m|sv|Britta}}, a contraction of {{m|sv|Birgitta}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1883.
From {{m|sv|bror||brother}}, a suitable name for a younger son.
From {{der|sv|de|Bruno}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Brynjulfr}}, from {{m|non|brynja||mail, armour}} + {{m|non|ulfr||wolf}}.
From {{der|sv|la|Camilla}} through literature. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1817.
Latinate form of {{m|sv|Karin}}. Can also be associated with {{der|sv|la|Carina}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1877.
{{der|sv|la|caritas||love}}. First appeared in the end of the 19th century; possibly inspired by the older names [[Carina]] and [[Marita]].
From {{der|sv|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Caecilia}}. First recorded in Sweden in the 12th century.
From {{der|sv|en|Charlie}}. First recorded as a Swedish name in 1872.
A short form of {{m|sv|Charlotta}} and a phonetic spelling of {{der|sv|fr|Charlotte}}.
Variant of {{m|sv|Christian}} through a medieval form ''Christiern''. First recorded in Sweden in 1484.
{{der+|sv|la|Chrīstiāna}}, {{m|la|Christina}}. First recorded in [[rune]]s as ''kristin'' in the 12th century. Name of a 17th century queen of Sweden.
English style spelling variant of the standard Swedish {{l|sv|Kristoffer}}.
Variant of {{m|sv|Claus}}, German short form of {{m|de|Nikolaus||[[Nicholas]]}}.
A 19th century variant of {{m|sv|Klara}}, possibly also inspired by the {{der|sv|fr|-}} surname, connected with 19th century Swedish royalty.
Used since the end of the nineteenth century. Explained in Sweden as an {{der|sv|en|-}} pet form of [[Constantine]] and [[Conrad]].
From {{der|sv|la|Cornelia}}. First recorded as a Swedish name in 1651.
From {{inh|sv|non|dagr||day}}, with identical meaning in modern Swedish. A [[runic]] name revived since 1863.
From {{inh|sv|non|Dagný}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Danr||a Dane}}.
From {{der|sv|la|Daniel}}, from {{der|sv|grc|Δᾱνῑήλ}}, from {{der|sv|he|דָּנִיֵּאל|tr=daniyél|lit=God is my judge}}, name borne from the prophet whose story is told in the Book of Daniel.
From Vulgate Latin {{m|la|Daniel}}, ultimately of {{der|sv|he|-}} origin. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1246.
A feminine form of {{m|sv|Daniel}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1819.
From {{der|sv|la-lat|Dāvīd}}, from {{der|sv|grc-koi|Δαυῑ̈́δ}}, from {{der|sv|hbo|דָּוִד|tr=dāwiḏ}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in [[rune]]s around 1200.

Borrowed from {{bor|sv|en|Dennis}} in the 20th century, from {{der|sv|fro|Denis}}, from {{der|sv|la|Dionȳsius}}, from {{der|sv|grc|Δῐονῡ́σῐος}}, from {{m|grc|Δῐόνῡσος}} + {{m|grc|-ῐος||belonging to}}, hence meaning ''follower of [[Dionysus]]''.
Introduced to Sweden by the early 19th century {{der|sv|fr|-}}-born queen {{l|fr|Désirée}} Bernadotte. Desirée is the most popular spelling in Sweden.

{{ety|sv|:bor|en:Dick}}
From {{bor|sv|en|Dick}}.

From {{der|sv|non|Dísa}}, short form of names containing the element {{m|non|dís||minor goddess}}. Name of a legendary Swedish queen, revived as a given name since 1788. Later also used as a diminutive of {{m|sv|Desirée}}.
From {{der|sv|en|Donald}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1880.
From {{bor|sv|da|-}}, shortened from {{m|da|Esbjørn}} (from {{der|sv|non|Ásbjǫrn}}) and {{m|da|Enbjørn}} (from {{cog|non|Arnbjørn}}).
From {{der|sv|en|Eddie}}. First recorded as a Swedish name in 1900.
{{bor+|sv|en|Edwin}}.
From {{bor|sv|de|Egon}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Einarr}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Eyvǫr}}, from a first part probably meaning "luck" ( same as in {{m|sv|Eivind}}) + {{m|non|vǫr||careful}}.
{{lbor|sv|non|Einarr}}, from {{der|sv|gem-pro|*ainaz||one}} and {{m|gem-pro|*harjaz||warrior}}. Cognate with {{cog|fo,is,nn|Einar}}, and {{cog|da|Ener}}. {{doublet|sv|Einar|Enar}}.
From {{der|sv|it|-}} and {{der|sv|es|-}} {{m|it|Elena}}.
Medieval vernacular form of {{m|sv|Helena}} (originally pronounced without the h in Swedish). First recorded in Sweden in the 14th century. Comparable to English [[Ellen]].
Latinate variant of {{l|sv|Elin}}.
Variant of {{m|sv|Elias}}.
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|en|Ellen}} and {{bor|sv|da|Ellen}}.
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|en|Ellinor}}.
From {{der|sv|en|Elliott}}.
Borrowed from the (American) {{bor|sv|en|Elmer}} in the 19th century.
From {{inh|sv|non|Eilífr}}, from elements meaning "always" / "alone" + "heir".

Rare medieval contraction of {{m|sv|Elisabet}}, also a variant Danish {{m|da|Else}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1422. Taken to general use in the 19th century through the influence of the identical German name.
From {{der|sv|it|-}} and {{der|sv|es|Elvira}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1808.
From {{der|sv|he|עִמָּנוּאֵל|tr=imanu'él}}, from {{m|he||עִמָּנוּ אֵל|lit=God is with us|tr=imánu él}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Embla}}.
From {{der|sv|fr|Émile}}, from {{der|sv|la|Aemilius}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1741.
From {{der|sv|de|Emma}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1766.
From {{inh|sv|non|Einarr}}, from {{der|sv|gem-pro|*ainaz||one}} and {{m|gem-pro|*harjaz||warrior}}. Cognate with {{cog|fo,is|Einar}}, {{cog|da|Ener}}, {{cog|nn|Einar}}.
From {{der|sv|de|Engelbrecht}}. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1305.

From {{der|sv|de|Engla}}, short form of {{der|sv|goh|-}} female compound names beginning with ''Engel-'', originally meaning an "[[Angle]]" but traditionally interpreted as "angel". First recorded as a Swedish given name as ''Engela'' in 1642.
From {{inh|sv|non|Eiríkr}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Eiríkr}}, from {{inh|sv|gmq-pro|*Aiwa-rikiaʀ|sc=Latn||lit=ever ruler}}.
Feminine form of {{m|sv|Erik}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1686 in the Latinate spelling {{m|sv|Erica}}.
{{der|sv|non|Erlingr}}
From {{der|sv|de|Erna}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1697.
From {{inh|sv|non|Ásbjǫrn}}, from {{m|non|[[áss]], [[óss]]||god}} + {{m|non|bjǫrn||bear}}.
Name of an 11th century Swedish saint, from {{der|sv|non|Áskell}}, ("god") + ("helmet", "cauldron").
{{der|sv|la|Eva}}, from {{der|sv|he|-}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1472.
Short form of {{m|sv|Evert}} and {{m|sv|Evald}}, also a masculine form of {{m|sv|Eva}}. First recorded as a Swedish given name in 1904.
Variant of {{m|sv|Eva}} and short form of {{m|sv|Evelina}}.
From {{der|sv|en|Evelyn}}, first recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1795. By [[folk etymology]] interpreted as a [[diminutive]] of {{m|sv|Eva}}.
From a [[Low German]] variant of [[German]] [[Eberhard]], cognate to English [[Everett]].
{{bor+|sv|en|Fanny}}.
From {{der|sv|la|Fēlīx}}.
{{der|sv|grc|-}} origin. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1581 as ''{{alter|sv|Philip}}''.

{{glossary|Affix}} of the first letters in {{m|sv|Filip}}, {{af|sv|Fil|l|-e|q2=[[gemination]]|q3=[[hypocoristic]] [[suffix]]}}.

{{der|sv|non|-}} ''[[Folki]]'', short form of names beginning with the element Folk- "people"; cognate to a medieval English given name surviving in the surnames [[Fulk]], [[Fulke]], [[Fawkes]] etc.
From {{bor|sv|de|Franz}}.
From {{bor|sv|en|Freddy}}.
From {{inh|sv|gmq-osw|Fredherik}}, of {{der|sv|gem}} origin, cognate with {{cog|en|Frederick}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1311.
{{lbor|sv|is|Freyr}}. {{m|sv|Frö}} is the etymologically correct form of the name.
From {{bor|sv|is|Freyja}}, from {{der|sv|gem-pro|*frawjǭ}}, ''Fröja'' or ''Fröa'' would be the expected form. Doublet of the second element in {{m|sv|hustru}}.
From {{der|sv|goh|fridu||peace}} + {{m|de|burg||[[fortress]]}}.
From {{der|sv|de|Fridolf}}, {{m|de|Friedolf}}, from {{der|sv|goh|fridu||peace}} + {{m|de|wolf||wolf}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1725.
From {{der|sv|non|Friðþjófr}}. Appears in Old Norse saga and was revived through 19th century literature. Cognate with {{cog|no|Fridtjof}} and {{cog|da|Frithjof}}.

From {{inh|sv|non|Gandalfr}}.
{{inh+|sv|gmq-osw|Georgius}}.
From {{der|sv|en|George}}. Variant of the standard Swedish {{m|sv|Georg}}. Both names ultimately derive from {{der|sv|grc|Γεώργιος}}, name of a legendary dragon-slaying saint.
From {{der|sv|non|Gerðr}}.

From {{der|sv|non|Geirmundr}}.

From {{der|sv|non|Guðmundr}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Guðrún}}.
From {{inh|sv|non|Gunnr}}, short form of female compound names with the element {{m|non|gunnr|t=battle}}. Name of a [[Valkyrie]] in Norse mythology. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1891.
{{der|sv|non|Gunnbjǫrg}}, from ''[[gunnr]]'' "battle" + ''[[bjǫrg]]'' "salvation".
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|de|Gunda}}. Cognate with {{cog|sv|Gun}}.
Via Danish, from {{inh|sv|non|Gundr}}, from {{der|sv|non|gunnr|gundr}}, from {{der|sv|gem-pro|*gunþiz||battle, war}}.

Latinized form of {{m|sv|Gunhild}}, borne by Swedish royalty. First recorded in Sweden as ''Gunnilda'' in 1473.

From {{der|sv|non|Gunnarr}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Gunnvǫr}}.

The oldest record in Sweden dates back to the year 1225 ("Gostauus"). In Peder Swart's chronicle about Gustav Vasa dated in the mid-1500s, the name is spelled Götstaff and is assumed to mean "Staff of the [[Geats]]."

From {{inh|sv|gmq-osw-lat|Iø̄rian}}, from {{w|Early Old Swedish}} {{m|gmq-osw|Iø̄ran}} or from {{bor|sv|gml|Jurian}}. Related to modern {{cog|de|Jürgen}} and {{cog|en|George}}. First recorded in Sweden as {{m|sv|Jöran}} in 1509.
{{inh|sv|non|Gauti}}, {{m|non|Gautr}} ("a [[Geat]]", "a resident of [[Götaland]]"), from {{inh|sv|gem-pro|*gautaz}}.
As a given name, often shortened from {{m|sv|Johanna}}, also derived from the biblical character(s). First recorded in Sweden in 1583.
From {{der|sv|en|Hannah}}, used as a modern spelling variant of the biblical Swedish {{m|sv|Hanna}}.
From {{bor|sv|de|Hans}}, a medieval [[short form]] of {{m|de|Johannes||[[John]]}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1356.
From {{inh|sv|non|Haraldr}}, from {{inh|sv|gem-pro|*Harjawaldaz}}.
From {{bor|sv|en|Harry}}.
From {{der|sv|de|Heidi}}.
From {{der|sv|grc|Ἑλένη|}}, cognate with English [[Helen]]. First recorded in Sweden in the 12th century.
From {{der|sv|fr|Hélène}}. First recorded as a Swedish name in 1810. Variant of {{m|sv|Helena||[[Helen]]}}.
From {{inh|sv|gmq-osw|Hiælgha}}, {{m|gmq-osw|Hælgha}}, from {{der|sv|non|Helga}}.
{{der|sv|non|Helgi}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Hemingr}}.

From {{der|sv|fr|Henriette}}, or borrowed from {{der|sv|en|-}}.
From {{inh|sv|gmq-osw|Henrik}}, of {{der|sv|gem}} origin, cognate with {{cog|de|Heinrich}} and {{cog|en|Henry}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1208.

{{der|sv|non|Hildingr}}, from {{m|non|hildingr||ruler, war chief}}. Made popular by a character in Tegnér's ''Fritiof's Saga''.
Borrowed from {{bor|sv|is|Hildur}} in the 19th century.
From {{der|sv|da|Helvig}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1482.
From {{der|sv|non|Hjalmarr}}, from {{m|non|hjalmr||helmet}} + {{m|non|herr||army}}.
Name of the mother of [[Sigurd]] in the [[Edda]]; from {{der|sv|non|Hjǫrdís}}.
From {{der|sv|da|Holger}}. Revived in the 19th century.
From {{der|sv|non|Hákon}}. Cognate with {{cog|fo|Hákun}}, {{cog|is|Hákon}}, {{cog|no|Håkon}} and {{cog|da|Hågen}}.
From {{der|sv|fr|Hélène}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1810.
From {{der|sv|de|Ida}}. First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1351, but not in general use before the 19th century.
From {{der|sv|he|עמנואל|tr=‘immánû ’Él}}, meaning ''God with us''.
Short form of names ending in -ina, such as {{m|sv|Sabina}}, {{m|sv|Severina}}, and of {{m|sv|Inez}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1836.
{{bor+|sv|en|Inez}}, from {{der|sv|es|Inés}}. First recorded as a given name of Swedes in 1842.
Shortened from {{m|sv|Inga}}, feminine form of {{m|sv|Inge}}.
From {{der|sv|non|Inga}}. Also recorded as a modern diminutive of {{l|sv|Ingeborg}} and {{l|sv|Ingrid}}.
From {{m|sv|Inga}} + {{m|sv|Lill}}, a pet form of [[Inga]], "little Inga", that came to regular use in early twentieth century.
From {{der|sv|non|Ingibjǫrg}}. In continuous use in Sweden since the early Middle Ages.

Originally a German diminutive of names beginning with the Germanic element ''Ingel-, Engel-'', in Sweden also used for ''Ing-'' names, such as [[Inga]] and [[Ingegerd]].
{{der|sv|non|Ingimarr}}, from ''Ingi''- ("the god [[Ing]]/[[Yngvi]]") and {{m|non|mærr}} ("famous").
Contraction of {{m|sv|Ingegerd}} and also a dialectal form of {{m|sv|Ingrid}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1561.
From {{der|sv|non|-}}.

From {{der|sv|de|Irma}}. First recorded in Sweden in 1868.

From {{bor|sv|da|Jens}}.
